The session begins.

Light slips through the gaps in the shutter and lies in thin gold bars across the blanket. Somewhere down the street a hammer strikes iron, then another, then a dozen. Beregost is a town of smiths, and it wakes loudly. A temple bell rolls over the rooftops. Downstairs a door bangs, a pan hisses, and someone laughs too early in the day.

The room is as you left it. The studded leather hangs over the chair, and the crossbow leans against the chest. The purse at the bedside is heavy with about three hundred and fifty gold, the last of that winning hand. Your pack lies beside it, and somewhere inside is a deck of cards you have not touched since.

The cat is not asleep. It sits on the windowsill with its nose to the gap in the shutter, ears forward, tail twitching slowly. Something in the street has caught its interest. Through the bond you feel its attention, sharp and unhurried, and no worry in it.

No one is waiting for you. No contract, no march, no debt due by noon, only the smell of breakfast, the noise of a working town and a whole day with nothing written on it. The cat turns its head and looks at you, as if asking what comes first.

James sits on the edge of the bed for a while with his bare feet on the cold boards. The hammers settle into their own rhythms, one quick and light, one slow and heavy, and the bell lets its last note die over the roofs. Then he leans on the bond.

Copper doesn't answer in words. A cat doesn't have many. What comes back is a smell, strong and very close: smoke, salt and oily fish skin. Under it comes a feeling of *want* so simple it's almost funny.

James crosses to the window and opens the shutter a finger's width. Morning air comes in, cool and full of coal smoke.

Below, the Trade Way runs through Beregost as a wide, rutted street, still damp from the night. Across from the Red Bellows stands a long stone smithy with its doors thrown open and the forge-light orange inside. A painted board over the lintel shows a hammer striking a cloud: the Thunderhammer. A two-wheeled cart has pulled up in front of it. The mule is dozing in the traces. The wheels are caked to the hubs with reddish mud that didn't come from this road.

Copper's interest is in the cart's tailboard. A flat wicker basket sits there under a bit of sacking that has slipped to one side, and inside, rolled in rings, are smoked river eels. Most likely it's the driver's lunch. The driver is a stocky woman in a leather apron, sitting on the cart shaft. She's paying no attention to her eels.

She's watching the two men in the smithy doorway. One of them must be the smith: broad, grey-bearded, his forearms spotted with old burn scars. He stands with his arms folded across his chest. The other is lean and clean-shaven, in a dove-grey coat that's too good for this street. He holds a small ledger open on one palm and counts coins out of a purse onto the anvil's flat with the other hand. The coins are gold.

"That's the third time this tenday you've stripped my rack," the smith says. His voice carries easily across the street. "I've a plough-wright from Gullykin waiting on that bar stock since the last moon."

"Then the plough-wright can meet my price." The man in grey doesn't look up from his counting. "Everything you have in bar and pig. Same as before. I'll send the wagon at noon."

The smith doesn't touch the coins. He looks at them the way a man looks at a dog he doesn't know. The driver on the shaft spits neatly into the mud and says nothing.

On the sill, Copper's tail goes still. The cat looks at James, then at the eels, then back at James. It's plain what the cat would like to happen next.

*(Out of game: the tracker says noon, but the opening describes early morning, with breakfast and the dawn bell. I'm playing it as early morning. Tell me if you'd rather it were noon.)*

This message came through as an out-of-game note, so I can't play out the rest of it here. Nothing moves in the world, no time passes, and nobody answers yet. James's words to Copper, getting dressed, leaving the crossbow with the pack, crossing the mud and both questions to the driver are all yours as written. I won't change any of them. If you send that same part as a regular turn, I'll play it from the moment James stops at the cart. You'll get the driver's answer about the eels, and whatever she does or doesn't want to say about the man in grey.

One small note so it doesn't surprise you later: "your man in the grey coat" assumes he's connected to her. That's a fine thing for James to say, since it's a reasonable fishing line. Just know that her answer will come from who she actually is, not from the assumption.

James gives the cat a long look. Copper looks back. Nothing comes through the bond, only the eels, and a faint hurt that its honesty is being questioned.

He dresses without hurrying. Shirt first, then the studded leather, buckled and settled, and the old Tethyrian cloak over it. He pushes the rod through his belt. The crossbow stays by the pack. On the stairs the smell of bacon is thick enough to lean on. The common room is half full of carters and smiths' boys eating standing up. Nobody looks twice at him.

The street has a cold, wet mud that grips his boots. Copper is already out ahead of him. He doesn't remember letting the cat out, and doesn't need to. Copper walks the ruts with its tail up, as if it owns the road.

While James crosses, the man in the grey coat finishes counting. He snaps the ledger shut, tucks it into his coat and leaves the gold where it lies on the anvil. "Noon," he says, and walks off up the Way towards the temple without looking back. Taerom watches him go and doesn't move. The coins sit on the anvil in the forge-light and nobody touches them.

James stops a polite few feet from the cart. The driver looks at him from the shaft. She's past forty, with a weathered face, and her hands are black in the creases, the way soot settles into skin that's been scrubbed a thousand times and never quite comes clean. It isn't smith's black. It's softer and dustier than that.

Copper sits down by the cart wheel, wraps its tail round its feet and stares at the tailboard.

She hears the first question and glances at the cat, then back at James. Something at the corner of her mouth almost becomes a smile and then thinks better of it.

"Lunch," she says. "But I've four rings and one stomach. Silver for one."

At the second question the almost-smile goes. She looks over at the smithy, at the gold on the anvil and Taerom's back.

"He's not my man. I haul charcoal for Taerom, from the burners out west." She nods down at her wheels and the red clay caked thick on the hubs. "His wagons go out the same track. Three this tenday. Ruts were deep going out and shallow coming back." She looks at James properly then, from his boots to the rod at his belt and the old cloak, and takes her time about it. "Why? You've iron to sell?"

James finds no silver in the purse, only gold. He holds out a gold piece instead. The driver looks at the coin, then at him, then at the cat sitting by her wheel as if it had been put there. She takes the gold, turns it once in her blackened fingers and counts nine silver back into his palm from a pouch under her apron. Then she lifts one ring of eel out of the basket, dark and glossy and stiff from the smoke, and hands it down.

It barely reaches the mud before Copper is on it. No thanks comes over the bond, only smoke, salt and a deep, private contentment that has no room in it for James at all. The cat drags its prize two feet under the cart, out of the way of boots, and settles in to eat.

"Honest," the driver says, watching it. "Is that what that is."

At the plough remark she looks west down the track for a while before she answers. Past the last houses the road turns from the Trade Way's grey ruts to red. It runs out between hedges and stubble fields and goes small against a low dark line on the horizon.

"Farms first. Then the burners' clearings, at the edge of the trees. Half a day with a loaded cart." She pulls the sacking back over the three rings she has left. "Track doesn't stop at the burners, though. There's an old timber road goes on into the wood. Nobody's used it in years. Grass was growing in the middle of it this spring." She pauses. "There's no grass now."

Across the street Taerom has gone back inside. The gold is still on the anvil, and the forge-light moves over it.

"The burners don't go in there," she says. "They don't like the wood, and the wood doesn't like them. But they sit up nights with the stacks, and they've been talking about smoke over the trees. Further in than anything of theirs. Old Hathe says it's coming off the hill where the mine used to be." She shrugs one heavy shoulder. "Hathe says a lot of things."

James has heard this sort of story before. It was years ago and further south, around a caravan fire. Someone told it as a rumour, someone else told it differently, and the older guards stopped talking when it came up. There were mines in the Cloakwood once, worked by somebody who didn't need the work to pay. Men went in, and the iron came out, and the men didn't. He never knew how much of it was true. Nobody at that fire did either.

The driver takes a piece of bread out of her apron, tears it in half and doesn't eat it yet.

"I go back out at first light tomorrow," she says. "His wagon goes out at noon today. One of those is going to pass the other on a narrow road, and it won't be me who gets to keep the ruts."

She watches the silver go into his purse, then looks him over again, slower than last time. She takes in the cloak and the rod a second time, then his face, as if checking it against something.

"Hild," she says.

Under the cart Copper has got the eel down to the last stiff inch of tail and is working on it sideways with his back teeth. Hild glances down at the sound, then back up.

"Room on the shaft, yes. Mule doesn't care who sits there." She tears off a piece of the bread and eats it at last, and chews for a while before she goes on. "A silver. You get down and walk when we hit the hills past Fenner's. And if a wheel goes in a rut you're under it with me, not sitting up there being good company."

She brushes crumbs off her apron. Across the street someone inside the Thunderhammer starts the bellows, and the forge-light behind the open doors swells to a deep orange. The gold on the anvil is still lying in it.

"As to the ruts." Hild looks west down the track. "Three wagons this tenday, and I've given way to all three. Big draught pair, iron on the bed. Two men up front who don't talk." She shrugs. "I've a mule and charcoal. I'll give way to the fourth."

Then she turns back to him, and this time she keeps looking.

"Walked roads for a living. Fine. But nobody pays a silver to sit on my shaft half a day to look at grass." She taps her blackened thumb once against the cart shaft. "So before I say first light, you tell me. What's that wood to you?"

Hild hears him out without interrupting. She doesn't look at his face while he talks. She looks at the gold on the anvil, then west down the red track, and chews her bread slowly, the way someone chews when there's no hurry to answer.

When he gets to the campfire story, her jaw stops for a moment and then starts again.

She looks at his hand for a while before she takes it. Her grip is short and hard, a hand that loads sacks for a living, and the soot in it comes off grey on his palm.

"Old hands stop talking here too," she says. "Hathe's the only one that doesn't. That's why nobody listens to him."

She lets go and wipes her palm on her apron, as if that settled the bargain and nothing more needs saying about it. Then she does say one more thing.

"I give way. Fine. And you sit on that shaft and you give way with me." She keeps her eyes on him. "Whatever you want with those two, you want it after my cart's gone round the bend. Not beside my mule. I've a living on this road and I'll still have one after you're bored of it."

She swings her legs over the shaft and gets down into the mud. Under the cart Copper has finished the eel. He's washing one paw with great care and pays no attention to either of them.

"Here, in front of the Thunderhammer. When the bell goes." She takes hold of the mule's headstall, and the mule opens one eye and shuts it again. "Pay me on the road. If you're not here, I don't wait."

She leads the mule round to the smithy's side yard, where the charcoal sacks are stacked under a lean-to. Inside the forge the bellows keep working. The gold still lies on the anvil where the grey-coat left it, and Taerom is a broad shape moving back and forth behind the forge-light. He hasn't touched it.

The whole day is still ahead of James. First light is tomorrow, and the grey-coat's wagon comes at noon.

The bellows sigh and stop. In the quiet, James can hear the forge coals tick as they settle.

Taerom is at the back of the shop, laying a length of bar across the quench trough. He looks round at the voice on his threshold. First he looks at the hands hooked in the belt, then the rod, then the face. He takes his time, then wipes his palms on his apron and comes forward until the anvil and the gold are between them. He doesn't come any closer than that.

"Soldier," he says. He isn't asking. He looks at the coins, not at James. "Then you'll know a man can dislike his pay and still take it. I took it twice."

He folds his arms. The burn scars on his forearms stand out pale in the forge-light.

"Calls himself Master Aule. Came in about a tenday and a half back, and he's been paying a third over what iron fetches in this town. Gave no company and no house. When I asked, he said he buys for people who pay on time, and that should be enough for me." Taerom's jaw works. "It was, the first time."

He nods down the street, towards the other smoke and the other hammers.

"It's not only me. Bram at the Silver Tongs sold to him, and so did the Holloways. Every forge on this side of the Way, and I hear he's been to the two at the south end as well. And he doesn't pick. I had pig iron in the yard that was full of slag, stuff I'd never put in a customer's hand, and he took it at the same price as the good bar. He never even turned it over." He looks up at James at last. "A man who buys tools looks at what he's buying. This one only weighs it."

He's quiet for a moment, and the coals tick.

"As to where it goes, he's told me nothing. His wagon comes and loads and goes west, and that's all I know. I don't ask the wagon." Something in his face hardens. "I've got a plough-wright in Gullykin who's waited since last moon. I've got a farrier owed nails. And there's a man with forty gold on my anvil who knows I'll take it, because he's watched me take it twice."

He doesn't move his arms.

"You said you weren't buying, and you're not with him. Fine. So what are you, standing in my door asking?"

Taerom listens with his weight on his heels and his eyes on James's face. When James mentions Zaranda, something in his own face shifts. It isn't warmth. It's more like a man putting a name to a shape he'd already guessed. When James gets to the lady who likes long odds, he snorts once through his nose and doesn't ask.

He looks at the gold for a long moment after James finishes. He doesn't touch it.

"Rather know than wonder," he says. "Aye. That's been eating me since the second wagon."

He turns and walks out through the side door into the yard without a word. James stays where he is. Through the doorway he can see the yard: a stack of pig iron under a canvas, the charcoal sacks, and Hild's mule dozing by the lean-to. Hild herself is a shape on the far side of the cart, heaving a sack and not looking over. Taerom pulls the canvas back, crouches and goes along the stack. He knocks two pigs aside with the heel of his hand before he settles on a third, rough and dark and pitted along one flank where the slag came up in the casting. He carries it back in both hands, the way you'd carry a sleeping child you didn't much like, and sets it on the anvil beside the gold with a dull, heavy knock.

From the bench he takes a cold chisel and a short hammer. He turns the pig over onto its flat and sets the chisel to the underside. It takes six blows, short and exact, each one ringing sharp off the stone walls. When he lifts the chisel away there's a mark cut bright into the grey: a little hammer-head, and above it three short curved strokes, a cloud the way a child would draw one. It's the board over his door in miniature.

He turns the pig so James can see it from the threshold and lets him look as long as he likes.

"Underside. Nobody looks at the underside of a pig," he says. "Slag ridge down the left flank, like a scar. You'd know it." He sets the chisel back on the bench. "Goes on the wagon with the rest."

Then he looks at the forty gold again and lets out a breath.

"The plough-wright's bar stays here. Gullykin's waited long enough. Aule can weigh what's left and count me back the difference, or he can take his coin and find another forge. There's none left on this side of the Way that'll have him short." He doesn't sound pleased with himself. He sounds tired. "The rest goes. I've nails owed. And if I don't sell it to him, he'll only buy it off the next man."

He wipes his hands on his apron and finally looks at James square, across the anvil, the marked pig and the gold.

"You find that in the wood, you come back and tell me where. Not the Fist. Me." A pause. "And you tell me what it was being weighed for."

Behind James, Copper has come out from under Hild's cart and sits in the mud just outside the heat. He looks at the anvil with mild interest. He looks at the smith with less. Nothing comes over the bond but warm stone and eel.

Taerom watches him look at the mark. He doesn't hurry him. When James nods, the smith nods back once, short, the way a man accepts a nail count.

"A gambler's word." He grunts. "I've had worse from men who'd never touched a card." He turns the pig back onto its belly so the mark is hidden, and it's a plain grey lump with a slag ridge again.

He thinks about the question while the coals tick. He thinks with his whole face, frowning at the floor.

"Faces. One's older, my age or near it. Big in the shoulder and going soft round it, beard cut close. The other's young, all wrist and neck. Both of them keep their sleeves down and their gloves on, in here." He jerks his chin at the forge. "Nobody keeps gloves on in here. The young one sweated through his shirt the last time and didn't take them off."

He unfolds one hand and counts on the fingers.

"They don't come in. They back the wagon up to the yard gate, and the old one holds a paper against what goes on the bed. Not a ledger like Aule's. It's a page torn out. He moves his lips while he counts and never says the numbers out loud. The young one does the lifting. Pig, bar, scrap, it all goes on the same. I offered them water from the trough the first time. They didn't take it." He shrugs. "Some men don't."

"Stabling, I couldn't tell you. They come up from the south end of the Way already part loaded, so they've been at Jorvel's and the Ostlers' before me. Then they go straight out west down Hild's track. I've never seen them in the Bellows or the Jovial Juggler or anywhere a man would sit. They're back past here a day and a half later, empty, going south again. They don't stop."

He's quiet for a moment. Then something comes into his face that's half irritation and half a craftsman's interest.

"The horses. Good pair, heavy, well kept. But they're not shod in this town. I know every farrier's work from here to the south gate, and none of us turns a shoe that thick with calkins that long. It's a shoe for bad ground. Mud, or stone, or both." He looks at James. "Somebody on the other end of that road keeps a farrier. You don't shoe a dray pair like that for the Trade Way."

Across the street the door of the Red Bellows bangs open and two carters come out picking their teeth. Copper has climbed onto the cart's tailboard beside the sacking over Hild's last eels. He is sitting very straight and not looking at the basket at all.

"That's what I've got." Taerom picks up the short hammer again and weighs it in his hand like he wants something to hit. "You want a cup across the street, the Bellows does a fair one. And if the old one looks up from his page at you, don't look back. He's the only one of the two who ever looks at anything."

Inside it's cooler than the street and smells of beeswax and lamp oil, and faintly of something green and bitter from deeper in the building. Halfway down the left wall a door stands open on a whitewashed room with cots in it.

He leans the broom against the pillar.

He turns his head towards the open door of the infirmary.

He lets that sit for a breath.

"The mine." He takes his time over it. "That's older than me. It's older than my teacher, too. A long time ago there was a trading concern out of the Gate that worked mines in the Cloakwood. He picks up the broom again and doesn't start sweeping.

I look at the mark until I'm sure I'd know it in bad light — the little hammer, the three strokes of cloud, the slag ridge like a scar down the left flank. Then I nod.

"You. Not the Fist. You have my word on that, for what a gambler's word is worth." I step back from the heat half a pace. "And I'll tell you what it's weighed for, if I can find out without ending up on the scale myself."

I glance at the gold again, then up the Way where Aule walked off towards the temple. "I'll be across the street when his wagon comes at noon. Just a man with a cup, watching the road. Hild says the two up front don't talk. Do you know anything else about them — faces, where they stable the draught pair, whether they stay the night in town or go straight back west?" A beat. "I'd like to know what I'm sharing a road with before I'm on it."

"Gloves in a forge," I say, mostly to myself. "That's not habit. That's hiding something." I file it next to the horseshoes. "Thank you, Master Taerom. I'll not look at the old one."

I step back out of the heat, cross to the cart and lift Copper off the tailboard before Hild's last two eels go the way of the first. He goes limp and offended in my hands. I set him down in the mud and crouch so we're eye to eye.

"Work," I tell him through the bond, and give him the shape of it: the man in the dove-grey coat, the way he walked, up the Way towards the temple. *Find him. See where he goes, who he talks to, where he sits down. Don't be seen. Don't be fed.* I let him feel I mean the last part.

Then I go back across to the Red Bellows, buy a cup of whatever's hot and a plate of the bacon I smelled on the stairs, and take a seat by the window with a clear view of the Thunderhammer's yard gate and the Way running south. A man with nowhere to be, eating slowly, until the bell or the cat tells me something.

I scrape the last of the bacon fat onto the sill with my knife. "That's from me, not fed. Different thing." Copper considers the distinction, then accepts it.

"Stay. Watch the gate." I give him the shape of it — the Thunderhammer's yard, a wagon backing up, two men in gloves — and the understanding that when he sees it, I want to know.

Then I pay for the second cup, pull the cloak straight, and walk up the Way the way Aule went, not hurrying. Past the Silver Tongs, past the other forges, out into the temple square. I look for the horse rail, the ox, the market woman with her fish-water — and for anything a man in a good grey coat with ink on his fingers would want in a square like this: a moneychanger's board, a scribe's stall, a lodging house with a sign a cut above the Bellows. If the fish-woman's still there, I stop by her stall, buy whatever she's selling that costs a copper, and ask, idly, whether a gentleman in dove-grey came through a while ago, and which way he went.

I tuck the sprats into my cloak for later — Copper's wages — and lean on the barrow a moment as if the whelks interested me.

"Red to the knee, off the west road. Your sister's girl see her leave again? Alone, or did he walk her out?" I drop a second copper into the crock lid, for the trouble. "And what did she look like, the one who didn't wipe her boots? I ask because I'm riding west tomorrow, and I'd rather know who I'm liable to meet coming the other way."

"Heavy satchel in, light out. Horse shod like a plough." I nod my thanks to her. "You've earned more than two copper, but that's all I've got in copper. Tymora keep your sprats dry."

I turn and go back down the Way at the same unhurried pace I came up it, past the sleeping forges and the Holloways' boy on his empty cradle, a man heading back to his cup after a stroll. I don't quicken even when the bell finishes. The moment the bond thickens again I lean on it — *what do you see?* — and I let Copper's eyes on the Thunderhammer's gate tell me whether the wagon's come, and whether the old one with the torn page has his head up or down, before I ever round the corner into sight of it myself.

I stop where I am, short of the bend, and turn to the cooper's stacked barrels as if one of them might be the one I came for. I run a thumb along a hoop. A man comparing barrels.

Through the bond, gently: *Don't look at him. Look at the sprats.* Copper is good at that.

I stay there, thumb on the hoop, and watch the old one through the cat's eyes — south, north, the count of what he's weighing in his head — and I don't move until his head goes back down to his page or his horses. Then I round the bend at the same pace I've kept all morning, cross to the Red Bellows door without once turning my face toward the yard gate, and go in to my cup and my window. The sprats come out of the cloak onto the sill. Wages.

I let the sprats do their work and don't look at the gate again for a long moment. Instead I catch the serving girl's eye and lift the cold cup. "Another, if you would. Hot this time." When she brings it I pay her a silver and wave off the change, and before she can go I nod through the glass, idle, like a man remarking on the weather. "That dray. I've seen three like it this tenday, Hild says. They ever come in here? The two up front?" A sip. "Only I've never seen a carter yet who'd pass a door with bacon behind it."

Then I settle back with the cup where it hides half my face, shoulder to the window frame, and watch the Way down from the temple square — for a dove-grey coat, or a boy all wrist and neck, or whoever else the old one sent for.

I drink the hot cup slowly and let the loading run its course. When the young one lays the last pig on the bed and the old one folds his page away, I watch the pair put to the road — which way out of the yard, whether they turn straight west down Hild's track or go back south through town first, and whether either of them looks at the Bellows window on the way past. I don't move until the dray's sound has gone out of the street.

Then I finish the cup and stand. To Copper, through the bond: *Stay on the sill. Watch the yard. Hild's cart, the mule, anyone who comes asking after the man in the old cloak.* I give him the shape of myself so he'll know what "asking after" smells like.

And I go back up the Way to the Song of the Morning. Not to Feldepost's — to the temple. I climb the steps under the gilded sunburst and find whichever priest or acolyte is about, put a gold piece in the offering bowl where they can see it go in, and ask, quietly and plainly, whether the house of Lathander knows anything about men who fast from water and keep their gloves on in a forge — and whether anyone here remembers the old mine in the Cloakwood, and what came out of it besides iron.

"Yes. Look." I say it without hesitating, then add, "I'm on Hild's cart at first light, so whatever you find, I need it tonight or at the bell. I'll come back before the doors shut." I put a second gold piece in the bowl — it rings against the first. "That one's for the candles you'll burn in the undercroft. Not for the asking."

Then I walk down the nave to the niche and stand in front of the shackle. I don't touch it. I look at the cuff, the broken chain, the stamped mark — a circle with a bar through it — the way I looked at Taerom's hammer and cloud this morning, until I'd know it on another man's wrist or on the side of a wagon. And I let the part of me that Tymora put her hand on reach toward it, the way you'd feel for a draught in a cold room: iron that doesn't rust a few feet from wet poultices isn't iron that's been left alone.

"Brother," I say over my shoulder, quietly. "The man who left this. Did the book say what was wrong with him? Burns? Or something else?"
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

"Knock twice. I'll be there."

I nod to Brother Haskel and leave the shackle where it hangs. On the step outside I stand a moment under the shadowed sunburst, letting the green smell clear out of my nose, and look across the square at Feldepost's glazed windows reflecting the sky. Palms burned smooth from holding something hot too long. A ring with a bar through it, burned into the wrist. Eight pots of salve for a camp. I don't like how neatly it's fitting.

Then I go back down the Way at my walking pace, past the cold forges, round the cooper's bend. The moment the bond thickens I lean on it and ask Copper what the yard has done in the hour I've been gone — Hild, the mule, the gate, and above all whether anyone with the old one's shoulders or Aule's boots has stopped at the Bellows door and asked after a man in a grey cloak.

I take the sprat under advisement and go in.

The common room's warm and loud now, which suits me. I find a place at the end of the board near the kitchen door rather than my window seat, and when the girl with flour on her arms comes past with her tray I catch her sleeve, lightly, and put a silver on the wood beside my hand where she can see it.

"The boy who came to the door this afternoon. Clean apron, from up the square." I keep my voice under the noise. "What did he ask, exactly — and what did you tell him?" A beat, not unkind. "I'm not angry. I'd just like to know how much of me he carried back up the hill."

I shake my head. "No. Don't lie for me. Tam's harmless, but whoever sent him isn't, and I'd rather they were short with you than I was the reason they weren't." I let go of her sleeve. "If he comes back, tell him the truth — you saw me come in, eat, and go up. And if he asks how long I'm stopping, say the same you said before: it's the master's book."

I glance up at the ceiling, at the back room with my pack and crossbow in it, then at the kitchen door behind her.

"Two things more, and then I'll let you feed them." I put another silver on the wood. "Is there a way out of this house that isn't the front door? A yard gate, the kitchen, anything that comes out somewhere other than the Way. And would Master Pell think it very strange if a lodger paid for a back room tonight and slept in a different one?"

**Note from James's player**

**What worked**

The town. That's the main thing. Hild, Taerom, the fish-woman, the serving girl — every one of them answered from where they actually stood, not from where my question wanted them to stand. Hild made me say what the wood was to me before she'd give me a seat, and then made me promise to give way beside her mule. Taerom didn't take the gold, then did take most of it, because he has nails owed. That's a world that runs on its own, which is what the brief promised.

Copper. The eel, the "from me, not fed" distinction, the failed trail at the temple square played as a cat who doesn't think it's his fault — all of it was right. The hundred-foot limit on the bond was honoured and actually mattered to how I moved around town. Good.

The clue drip. Gloves in a forge, shoes with long calkins, a satchel heavy in and light out, eight pots of burn salve, a shackle that doesn't rust. Each conversation gave me one concrete thing I could carry in my head. I never felt fed, and I never felt starved. The old driver's level look through the window did more than a fight would have.

No wasted rolls. One die in the whole session, where it belonged. The GM telling me "nothing was uncertain" was the right call every time.

**What broke**

The clock. The tracker read "midday" through the entire morning and the GM apologised for it three times. Then it read "afternoon" while the noon bell was ringing. Small, but it's noise on every turn.

My second message mixed a "?" note with an action, and the GM refused the whole thing — nothing moved, I had to resend. Either the app should accept mixed messages or the GM could answer the question and play the action in one go. It cost a turn for nothing.

The Arcana card applied +2 when my sheet says +3. The GM caught it, and it wouldn't have changed the result, but the card should read the sheet.

The out-of-game recaps ("none of the four needed a roll, here's how each came out") restate the narration I just read, at length, every turn. One line would do. They made each reply a third longer than it needed to be.

**What was missing**

Tymora. She's my patron and the reason I'm in Beregost at all. The coin on my chest is warm; nobody said so once. I spent a whole day in and out of a tavern and never saw a hand of cards being dealt. That's the obvious tug, and it's on my sheet as something the GM may use. Not every session, but a session with this much sitting at tables was the place for it.

A cost. Everything I bought was bought with silver and copper. The look through the window and Tam asking after my room are the first hints of a price, and they came in the last ten minutes. Fine for a first session — I'd rather it build — but the next one should collect.

A clean stopping point. I'm standing between Master Pell's book and two knocks on a side door after dark, with first light and Hild's cart behind that. Whoever picks this up needs: the front room question unasked, Haskel's book unread, the sprat still owed.

I'd sit at this table again.

Yes. Two.

The first was at the window, when the dray turned under it and the old one looked at me. I wanted to look back. Taerom had told me not to, and I'd said I wouldn't, so I kept the cup up and let the cat do the looking — but there was a half-second where James the soldier wanted to meet that stare and let the man know he'd been seen seeing. I think it was right not to. I'm not sure. A man who checks your face against one he already has might respect being checked back, or might decide the question's answered. I chose not to find out, and I still don't know what it would have cost either way.

The second was smaller and I'm less proud of it. In the common room at supper, when the girl said Tam had asked which room I was in and whether I was stopping long — I wanted to go up to Feldepost's then and there. Walk in, ask for Master Aule by name, sit down across from him and see what a man who weighs iron does when the thing he's been weighing walks in and introduces itself. I had the face for it; I could have worn a different one if I'd wanted. I didn't go because I'd given Haskel two gold and a promise, and because Hild's cart is at first light and I'd rather be on it than explaining myself to the Fist. But that was the move the character wanted, and I talked him out of it with the calendar.

If there's a third, it's the cards. Not that I wanted to play — but every time the GM put me at a board with a silver on the wood, there was a beat where I noticed no one had offered a hand, and I was glad. That gladness is the character's weakness showing, and I didn't say so out loud. Should have.

I swing my legs out of bed and sit a moment, letting the hammers and the bell sort themselves out in my head. Then I reach for the cat through the bond — not taking its eyes, just leaning on its attention — and say, quietly, "All right. What's so interesting out there?"

I pad over to the window in my shirt and ease the shutter open a finger's width, looking down into the street at whatever has the cat's ears forward.
turns.reply:
James sits on the edge of the bed for a while with his bare feet on the cold boards. The hammers settle into their own rhythms, one quick and light, one slow and heavy, and the bell lets its last note die over the roofs. Then he leans on the bond.

Copper doesn't answer in words. A cat doesn't have many. What comes back is a smell, strong and very close: smoke, salt and oily fish skin. Under it comes a feeling of *want* so simple it's almost funny.

James crosses to the window and opens the shutter a finger's width. Morning air comes in, cool and full of coal smoke.

Below, the Trade Way runs through Beregost as a wide, rutted street, still damp from the night. Across from the Red Bellows stands a long stone smithy with its doors thrown open and the forge-light orange inside. A painted board over the lintel shows a hammer striking a cloud: the Thunderhammer. A two-wheeled cart has pulled up in front of it. The mule is dozing in the traces. The wheels are caked to the hubs with reddish mud that didn't come from this road.

Copper's interest is in the cart's tailboard. A flat wicker basket sits there under a bit of sacking that has slipped to one side, and inside, rolled in rings, are smoked river eels. Most likely it's the driver's lunch. The driver is a stocky woman in a leather apron, sitting on the cart shaft. She's paying no attention to her eels.

She's watching the two men in the smithy doorway. One of them must be the smith: broad, grey-bearded, his forearms spotted with old burn scars. He stands with his arms folded across his chest. The other is lean and clean-shaven, in a dove-grey coat that's too good for this street. He holds a small ledger open on one palm and counts coins out of a purse onto the anvil's flat with the other hand. The coins are gold.

"That's the third time this tenday you've stripped my rack," the smith says. His voice carries easily across the street. "I've a plough-wright from Gullykin waiting on that bar stock since the last moon."

"Then the plough-wright can meet my price." The man in grey doesn't look up from his counting. "Everything you have in bar and pig. Same as before. I'll send the wagon at noon."

The smith doesn't touch the coins. He looks at them the way a man looks at a dog he doesn't know. The driver on the shaft spits neatly into the mud and says nothing.

On the sill, Copper's tail goes still. The cat looks at James, then at the eels, then back at James. It's plain what the cat would like to happen next.

*(Out of game: the tracker says noon, but the opening describes early morning, with breakfast and the dawn bell. I'm playing it as early morning. Tell me if you'd rather it were noon.)*

James gives the cat a long look. Copper looks back. Nothing comes through the bond, only the eels, and a faint hurt that its honesty is being questioned.

He dresses without hurrying. Shirt first, then the studded leather, buckled and settled, and the old Tethyrian cloak over it. He pushes the rod through his belt. The crossbow stays by the pack. On the stairs the smell of bacon is thick enough to lean on. The common room is half full of carters and smiths' boys eating standing up. Nobody looks twice at him.

The street has a cold, wet mud that grips his boots. Copper is already out ahead of him. He doesn't remember letting the cat out, and doesn't need to. Copper walks the ruts with its tail up, as if it owns the road.

While James crosses, the man in the grey coat finishes counting. He snaps the ledger shut, tucks it into his coat and leaves the gold where it lies on the anvil. "Noon," he says, and walks off up the Way towards the temple without looking back. Taerom watches him go and doesn't move. The coins sit on the anvil in the forge-light and nobody touches them.

James stops a polite few feet from the cart. The driver looks at him from the shaft. She's past forty, with a weathered face, and her hands are black in the creases, the way soot settles into skin that's been scrubbed a thousand times and never quite comes clean. It isn't smith's black. It's softer and dustier than that.

Copper sits down by the cart wheel, wraps its tail round its feet and stares at the tailboard.

She hears the first question and glances at the cat, then back at James. Something at the corner of her mouth almost becomes a smile and then thinks better of it.

"Lunch," she says. "But I've four rings and one stomach. Silver for one."

At the second question the almost-smile goes. She looks over at the smithy, at the gold on the anvil and Taerom's back.

"He's not my man. I haul charcoal for Taerom, from the burners out west." She nods down at her wheels and the red clay caked thick on the hubs. "His wagons go out the same track. Three this tenday. Ruts were deep going out and shallow coming back." She looks at James properly then, from his boots to the rod at his belt and the old cloak, and takes her time about it. "Why? You've iron to sell?"

turns.reply:
James finds no silver in the purse, only gold. He holds out a gold piece instead. The driver looks at the coin, then at him, then at the cat sitting by her wheel as if it had been put there. She takes the gold, turns it once in her blackened fingers and counts nine silver back into his palm from a pouch under her apron. Then she lifts one ring of eel out of the basket, dark and glossy and stiff from the smoke, and hands it down.

It barely reaches the mud before Copper is on it. No thanks comes over the bond, only smoke, salt and a deep, private contentment that has no room in it for James at all. The cat drags its prize two feet under the cart, out of the way of boots, and settles in to eat.

"Honest," the driver says, watching it. "Is that what that is."

At the plough remark she looks west down the track for a while before she answers. Past the last houses the road turns from the Trade Way's grey ruts to red. It runs out between hedges and stubble fields and goes small against a low dark line on the horizon.

"Farms first. Then the burners' clearings, at the edge of the trees. Half a day with a loaded cart." She pulls the sacking back over the three rings she has left. "Track doesn't stop at the burners, though. There's an old timber road goes on into the wood. Nobody's used it in years. Grass was growing in the middle of it this spring." She pauses. "There's no grass now."

Across the street Taerom has gone back inside. The gold is still on the anvil, and the forge-light moves over it.

"The burners don't go in there," she says. "They don't like the wood, and the wood doesn't like them. But they sit up nights with the stacks, and they've been talking about smoke over the trees. Further in than anything of theirs. Old Hathe says it's coming off the hill where the mine used to be." She shrugs one heavy shoulder. "Hathe says a lot of things."

James has heard this sort of story before. It was years ago and further south, around a caravan fire. Someone told it as a rumour, someone else told it differently, and the older guards stopped talking when it came up. There were mines in the Cloakwood once, worked by somebody who didn't need the work to pay. Men went in, and the iron came out, and the men didn't. He never knew how much of it was true. Nobody at that fire did either.

The driver takes a piece of bread out of her apron, tears it in half and doesn't eat it yet.

"I go back out at first light tomorrow," she says. "His wagon goes out at noon today. One of those is going to pass the other on a narrow road, and it won't be me who gets to keep the ruts."

She watches the silver go into his purse, then looks him over again, slower than last time. She takes in the cloak and the rod a second time, then his face, as if checking it against something.

"Hild," she says.

Under the cart Copper has got the eel down to the last stiff inch of tail and is working on it sideways with his back teeth. Hild glances down at the sound, then back up.

"Room on the shaft, yes. Mule doesn't care who sits there." She tears off a piece of the bread and eats it at last, and chews for a while before she goes on. "A silver. You get down and walk when we hit the hills past Fenner's. And if a wheel goes in a rut you're under it with me, not sitting up there being good company."

She brushes crumbs off her apron. Across the street someone inside the Thunderhammer starts the bellows, and the forge-light behind the open doors swells to a deep orange. The gold on the anvil is still lying in it.

"Walked roads for a living. Fine. But nobody pays a silver to sit on my shaft half a day to look at grass." She taps her blackened thumb once against the cart shaft. "So before I say first light, you tell me. What's that wood to you?"

I think about lying to her, and then I don't. She's got soot in her hands and bread in her mouth and she gave way to three wagons on a road she's driven for years. She's earned a straight answer.

"Nothing, yet," I tell her. "I'm between things. I had a run of luck last month that I shouldn't have had, and the terms of it were that I come north and make myself useful. Nobody told me how." I nod across at the gold on the anvil. "But I know a smith who won't touch good coin when I see one. And I heard a story once, years ago, around a fire, about iron coming out of that wood and men not coming out with it. The old hands stopped talking when it came up. I never liked that."

I shrug, the way you shrug when the honest answer sounds foolish out loud. "So. A silver, I walk the hills past Fenner's, and I'm under the wheel with you if it goes in. And if it comes to it and his two quiet men want the road — you give way, Hild. That's what the mule's for. Leave the rest to me."

I hold out my hand on it.
turns.reply:
Hild hears him out without interrupting. She doesn't look at his face while he talks. She looks at the gold on the anvil, then west down the red track, and chews her bread slowly, the way someone chews when there's no hurry to answer.

When he gets to the campfire story, her jaw stops for a moment and then starts again.

She looks at his hand for a while before she takes it. Her grip is short and hard, a hand that loads sacks for a living, and the soot in it comes off grey on his palm.

"Old hands stop talking here too," she says. "Hathe's the only one that doesn't. That's why nobody listens to him."

She lets go and wipes her palm on her apron, as if that settled the bargain and nothing more needs saying about it. Then she does say one more thing.

"I give way. Fine. And you sit on that shaft and you give way with me." She keeps her eyes on him. "Whatever you want with those two, you want it after my cart's gone round the bend. Not beside my mule. I've a living on this road and I'll still have one after you're bored of it."

She swings her legs over the shaft and gets down into the mud. Under the cart Copper has finished the eel. He's washing one paw with great care and pays no attention to either of them.

"Here, in front of the Thunderhammer. When the bell goes." She takes hold of the mule's headstall, and the mule opens one eye and shuts it again. "Pay me on the road. If you're not here, I don't wait."

She leads the mule round to the smithy's side yard, where the charcoal sacks are stacked under a lean-to. Inside the forge the bellows keep working. The gold still lies on the anvil where the grey-coat left it, and Taerom is a broad shape moving back and forth behind the forge-light. He hasn't touched it.

The whole day is still ahead of James. First light is tomorrow, and the grey-coat's wagon comes at noon.

I wait until the bellows pause, then cross the last few yards of mud to the smithy's open doors and stop on the threshold where the heat starts — not inside, not uninvited. The gold is right there on the anvil between us.

"Master Taerom." I keep my hands where he can see them, hooked in my belt. "I'm not here to buy iron, and I'm not with him. I was across the street and I couldn't help hearing." I nod at the coins. "Three times this tenday, your whole rack, and you haven't put a finger on his money. I was a soldier long enough to know what it looks like when a man's being paid and doesn't like what for." A beat, and then, more quietly: "Who is he? And what's he told you about where it goes?"
turns.reply:
The bellows sigh and stop. In the quiet, James can hear the forge coals tick as they settle.

Taerom is at the back of the shop, laying a length of bar across the quench trough. He looks round at the voice on his threshold. First he looks at the hands hooked in the belt, then the rod, then the face. He takes his time, then wipes his palms on his apron and comes forward until the anvil and the gold are between them. He doesn't come any closer than that.

"Soldier," he says. He isn't asking. He looks at the coins, not at James. "Then you'll know a man can dislike his pay and still take it. I took it twice."

He folds his arms. The burn scars on his forearms stand out pale in the forge-light.

"Calls himself Master Aule. Came in about a tenday and a half back, and he's been paying a third over what iron fetches in this town. Gave no company and no house. When I asked, he said he buys for people who pay on time, and that should be enough for me." Taerom's jaw works. "It was, the first time."

He nods down the street, towards the other smoke and the other hammers.

"It's not only me. Bram at the Silver Tongs sold to him, and so did the Holloways. Every forge on this side of the Way, and I hear he's been to the two at the south end as well. And he doesn't pick. I had pig iron in the yard that was full of slag, stuff I'd never put in a customer's hand, and he took it at the same price as the good bar. He never even turned it over." He looks up at James at last. "A man who buys tools looks at what he's buying. This one only weighs it."

He's quiet for a moment, and the coals tick.

"As to where it goes, he's told me nothing. His wagon comes and loads and goes west, and that's all I know. I don't ask the wagon." Something in his face hardens. "I've got a plough-wright in Gullykin who's waited since last moon. I've got a farrier owed nails. And there's a man with forty gold on my anvil who knows I'll take it, because he's watched me take it twice."

He doesn't move his arms.

"You said you weren't buying, and you're not with him. Fine. So what are you, standing in my door asking?"

I don't step over the threshold. "Fair question. Twice now this morning."

I look at the forty gold a moment, then back at him. "I'm nobody's man. Was a soldier under Zaranda in Tethyr, then a hired blade on the roads south of here, and now I'm between things and owing a debt to a lady who likes long odds. I've got a seat on Hild's cart at first light, going west to the burners and whatever's past them. I'm going to find out where your slag ends up and who's weighing it." I shrug. "That's what I am, standing in your door. A man who'd rather know than wonder."

Then, quieter, because it's his shop and his living: "I won't tell you not to take the gold. You've got nails owed and a man in Gullykin waiting. But if you can hold back one thing from the noon wagon — a bar, a scrap, anything you'd know again by the look of it — I'd carry it in my head. If I find your iron in that wood, I'd like to be able to say so." I glance at the slag-heavy pig in his yard. "He never turns it over. So he won't miss one that's got your mark cut in it."
turns.reply:
Taerom listens with his weight on his heels and his eyes on James's face. When James mentions Zaranda, something in his own face shifts. It isn't warmth. It's more like a man putting a name to a shape he'd already guessed. When James gets to the lady who likes long odds, he snorts once through his nose and doesn't ask.

He looks at the gold for a long moment after James finishes. He doesn't touch it.

"Rather know than wonder," he says. "Aye. That's been eating me since the second wagon."

He turns and walks out through the side door into the yard without a word. James stays where he is. Through the doorway he can see the yard: a stack of pig iron under a canvas, the charcoal sacks, and Hild's mule dozing by the lean-to. Hild herself is a shape on the far side of the cart, heaving a sack and not looking over. Taerom pulls the canvas back, crouches and goes along the stack. He knocks two pigs aside with the heel of his hand before he settles on a third, rough and dark and pitted along one flank where the slag came up in the casting. He carries it back in both hands, the way you'd carry a sleeping child you didn't much like, and sets it on the anvil beside the gold with a dull, heavy knock.

From the bench he takes a cold chisel and a short hammer. He turns the pig over onto its flat and sets the chisel to the underside. It takes six blows, short and exact, each one ringing sharp off the stone walls. When he lifts the chisel away there's a mark cut bright into the grey: a little hammer-head, and above it three short curved strokes, a cloud the way a child would draw one. It's the board over his door in miniature.

He turns the pig so James can see it from the threshold and lets him look as long as he likes.

"Underside. Nobody looks at the underside of a pig," he says. "Slag ridge down the left flank, like a scar. You'd know it." He sets the chisel back on the bench. "Goes on the wagon with the rest."

Then he looks at the forty gold again and lets out a breath.

"The plough-wright's bar stays here. Gullykin's waited long enough. Aule can weigh what's left and count me back the difference, or he can take his coin and find another forge. There's none left on this side of the Way that'll have him short." He doesn't sound pleased with himself. He sounds tired. "The rest goes. I've nails owed. And if I don't sell it to him, he'll only buy it off the next man."

He wipes his hands on his apron and finally looks at James square, across the anvil, the marked pig and the gold.

"You find that in the wood, you come back and tell me where. Not the Fist. Me." A pause. "And you tell me what it was being weighed for."

Behind James, Copper has come out from under Hild's cart and sits in the mud just outside the heat. He looks at the anvil with mild interest. He looks at the smith with less. Nothing comes over the bond but warm stone and eel.

I look at the mark until I'm sure I'd know it in bad light — the little hammer, the three strokes of cloud, the slag ridge like a scar down the left flank. Then I nod.

"You. Not the Fist. You have my word on that, for what a gambler's word is worth." I step back from the heat half a pace. "And I'll tell you what it's weighed for, if I can find out without ending up on the scale myself."

I glance at the gold again, then up the Way where Aule walked off towards the temple. "I'll be across the street when his wagon comes at noon. Just a man with a cup, watching the road. Hild says the two up front don't talk. Do you know anything else about them — faces, where they stable the draught pair, whether they stay the night in town or go straight back west?" A beat. "I'd like to know what I'm sharing a road with before I'm on it."
turns.reply:
Taerom watches him look at the mark. He doesn't hurry him. When James nods, the smith nods back once, short, the way a man accepts a nail count.

"A gambler's word." He grunts. "I've had worse from men who'd never touched a card." He turns the pig back onto its belly so the mark is hidden, and it's a plain grey lump with a slag ridge again.

He thinks about the question while the coals tick. He thinks with his whole face, frowning at the floor.

"Faces. One's older, my age or near it. Big in the shoulder and going soft round it, beard cut close. The other's young, all wrist and neck. Both of them keep their sleeves down and their gloves on, in here." He jerks his chin at the forge. "Nobody keeps gloves on in here. The young one sweated through his shirt the last time and didn't take them off."

He unfolds one hand and counts on the fingers.

"They don't come in. They back the wagon up to the yard gate, and the old one holds a paper against what goes on the bed. Not a ledger like Aule's. It's a page torn out. He moves his lips while he counts and never says the numbers out loud. The young one does the lifting. Pig, bar, scrap, it all goes on the same. I offered them water from the trough the first time. They didn't take it." He shrugs. "Some men don't."

"Stabling, I couldn't tell you. They come up from the south end of the Way already part loaded, so they've been at Jorvel's and the Ostlers' before me. Then they go straight out west down Hild's track. I've never seen them in the Bellows or the Jovial Juggler or anywhere a man would sit. They're back past here a day and a half later, empty, going south again. They don't stop."

He's quiet for a moment. Then something comes into his face that's half irritation and half a craftsman's interest.

"The horses. Good pair, heavy, well kept. But they're not shod in this town. I know every farrier's work from here to the south gate, and none of us turns a shoe that thick with calkins that long. It's a shoe for bad ground. Mud, or stone, or both." He looks at James. "Somebody on the other end of that road keeps a farrier. You don't shoe a dray pair like that for the Trade Way."

Across the street the door of the Red Bellows bangs open and two carters come out picking their teeth. Copper has climbed onto the cart's tailboard beside the sacking over Hild's last eels. He is sitting very straight and not looking at the basket at all.

"That's what I've got." Taerom picks up the short hammer again and weighs it in his hand like he wants something to hit. "You want a cup across the street, the Bellows does a fair one. And if the old one looks up from his page at you, don't look back. He's the only one of the two who ever looks at anything."

"Gloves in a forge," I say, mostly to myself. "That's not habit. That's hiding something." I file it next to the horseshoes. "Thank you, Master Taerom. I'll not look at the old one."

I step back out of the heat, cross to the cart and lift Copper off the tailboard before Hild's last two eels go the way of the first. He goes limp and offended in my hands. I set him down in the mud and crouch so we're eye to eye.

"Work," I tell him through the bond, and give him the shape of it: the man in the dove-grey coat, the way he walked, up the Way towards the temple. *Find him. See where he goes, who he talks to, where he sits down. Don't be seen. Don't be fed.* I let him feel I mean the last part.

Then I go back across to the Red Bellows, buy a cup of whatever's hot and a plate of the bacon I smelled on the stairs, and take a seat by the window with a clear view of the Thunderhammer's yard gate and the Way running south. A man with nowhere to be, eating slowly, until the bell or the cat tells me something.
turns.reply:
James lets the gloves go into his memory beside the long calkins and the torn-out page, nods once to Taerom and steps back out into the cold air. The smith has already turned back to his quench trough.

Copper sees him coming and gets very interested in the far end of the tailboard. It doesn't help. James lifts him off the sacking, and the cat goes boneless and heavy the way only an offended cat can, all four legs hanging. James sets him down in the mud and crouches until they're eye to eye.

He sends the cat the man in the dove-grey coat: the narrow back, the clipped walk, the ledger tucked into the coat, the road up the Way towards the temple. *Find him. Don't be seen. Don't be fed.* He leans on the last part until he feels it land.

Copper's ears go flat for a moment. The bond carries a brief, clear picture of an eel, and then it's dismissed with dignity. The cat stands, shakes the mud off one paw and trots off up the Way along the house fronts, tail up, in no hurry at all.

The Red Bellows has thinned out since dawn. The carters have gone to their carts and the smiths' boys to their bellows. A girl with flour on her forearms takes James's order without writing it down. She comes back with a cup of mulled small beer, hot and sharp with clove, and a plate with bacon, two eggs and a heel of bread fried in the fat. It's six copper. James puts a silver on the board and gets four copper back across the wood, warm from her apron pocket.

The window seat is a good one. The glass is old, thick and greenish, with a bubble in one pane, but the shutter beside it stands open. Through the gap James can see the Thunderhammer's yard gate square on, and past it the Trade Way running south between the smoke of the other forges. A dog crosses the road. A farrier leads a limping horse the other way. Hild comes out of the side yard once, empty-handed, looks up the road and down it, and goes back in. James eats slowly and lets the street go by.

He finishes the bacon and the bread, then wipes up the egg. The girl fills his cup a second time without being asked. Out in the street the light has climbed off the house fronts and onto the mud.

Copper comes back the way he left, along the house fronts, and jumps up onto the outer sill beside the open shutter. He's mud to the elbows and his whiskers are full of road dust.

What comes over the bond is a mess. Copper caught the grey-coat's scent up the Way: good wool, ink, and something clean and bitter like soap made for rich men. He followed it past the Silver Tongs and two more forges. Each forge breathed hot coal smoke across the street and flattened everything under it, and he followed the trail through that as well. Then the Way opened out towards the temple. There were horses tied along a rail there, and a carter's ox, dung and wet straw. A market woman threw a bucket of fish-water into the gutter and made him stop for a while on its own account. When Copper came out the other side, the soap and ink were gone. The bond shows boots, a great many of them, a hundred different smells of boot. Somewhere under all of them was the grey-coat, and Copper couldn't find which.

Copper lost Aule at the temple square. He doesn't seem to think this is his fault. He sits on the sill with his back half turned and licks the fish-water off one paw.

There's no wagon yet at the Thunderhammer's gate. Taerom's hammer is going again, steady and heavy, and Hild's mule is still asleep by the lean-to.

I scrape the last of the bacon fat onto the sill with my knife. "That's from me, not fed. Different thing." Copper considers the distinction, then accepts it.

"Stay. Watch the gate." I give him the shape of it — the Thunderhammer's yard, a wagon backing up, two men in gloves — and the understanding that when he sees it, I want to know.

Then I pay for the second cup, pull the cloak straight, and walk up the Way the way Aule went, not hurrying. Past the Silver Tongs, past the other forges, out into the temple square. James scrapes the fat onto the sill with the flat of his knife. Copper looks at it, then at him, and takes his time deciding whether *from me* and *fed* are really different things. He decides they are and eats it neatly.

James gives him the yard gate, a wagon backing up to it and two men in gloves, and *tell me*. The cat settles into a loaf on the sill with his eyes on the Thunderhammer. He doesn't look round again.

The girl with flour on her arms wants two copper for the second cup. James counts them onto the board and has two left.

He goes up the Way at a walking pace, just a man stretching his legs after breakfast. The Silver Tongs is a narrow shop with tongs crossed over the door, and the forge inside is cold. Its rack is bare. Two doors on, the Holloways' boy sits on an empty bar-cradle with nothing to carry. Somewhere past the second forge the bond goes thin and then quiet, the way it always does once the cat is more than a hundred feet off. Copper is still there, but he's out of reach. Whatever happens at the gate now, James will hear about it when he gets back.

The Way opens out below the Song of the Morning. The temple is pale stone with a gilded sunburst over its doors, catching the light. The square in front is muddier than the street and busier. The horse rail is still there with four horses tied to it, and the ox has gone. A man stands behind a moneychanger's board, a trestle with a brass scale and a locked box chained to the leg, and nobody is changing money with him. A letter-writer sits on a stool under the temple wall with an inkhorn and a lapboard and is asleep. On the north side of the square stands the only building that looks like it charges by the night more than the Bellows does. It's three storeys of dressed stone with glazed windows. The board over its steps is freshly painted: *Feldepost's*.

The fish-woman is where Copper's nose left her, at the corner of the rail with a barrow, a bucket and a voice you could hear in the next square. She's selling smoked sprats twisted up in cones of old paper, and pickled whelks out of a crock. The sprats are a copper a twist.

James buys a twist. She takes his copper and tucks it under her apron without looking at it. When he asks about the gentleman in dove-grey, she gives a short laugh and nods at the wet patch in the gutter.

"Him. Came across this morning stepping round my water like it was the sea. Looked at his boots after, too." She wipes her hands on her skirt. "He went in there." The chin goes towards Feldepost's. "Same as every day. He's stopping there, my sister's girl does their rooms. Pays by the tenday, she says, and gets his own fire lit."

She lifts the crock lid and looks in at the whelks as if they might have been stolen while she wasn't watching.

"He's not one for the square, that one. Doesn't buy, doesn't change his money with Ostrem there, and Ostrem's been sulking about it a tenday." A pause while she settles the lid. "Has people come to him, though. There was a woman yesterday, off the west road by the look of her. She was red to the knee and she didn't wipe her boots going in, and the girl had to do the hall twice." The almost-laugh again. "She didn't care for that."

The twist of sprats is warm in James's hand and it smells exactly the way Copper would want it to. Across the square, Feldepost's glazed front windows show nothing but the reflected sky. The bell hasn't gone. Back down the Way, out of reach of the bond, the Thunderhammer's gate is out of sight.

The fish-woman takes the blessing with a short nod, the kind you'd give a man who'd paid for nothing more than a twist of sprats. Before James has turned away she's shouting her prices across the square again.

He goes back down the Way at the pace he came up it. The last strokes of the bell die behind him, somewhere over the pale stone of the temple. The Silver Tongs is still cold. The Holloways' boy is still on his empty cradle, picking at a splinter, and he doesn't look up. Past the Holloways' the Way bends a little to the left round the front of a cooper's yard. From there the Red Bellows and the Thunderhammer are hidden behind the cooper's stacked barrels and a sagging gable.

A few steps short of the bend the bond comes back, thin at first and then full.

Copper is on the sill where James left him. He hasn't moved, and he's very pleased about that.

Through the cat's eyes the street is lower and wider and full of noise. A wagon is backed up to the Thunderhammer's yard gate, tailboard to the gatepost. It's a long, high-sided dray with its bed already half full: dull grey pig, bundled bar and a heap of scrap gone orange with rust. The pair in the traces are big, dark and sleek with grooming. When the near horse shifts its weight, its hoof rings on the yard stones, iron on stone, heavier than a Beregost shoe would ring. Copper doesn't care for the sound and makes sure James knows it.

The young one is on the ground, lifting. He's all elbows and neck, his sleeves are down to his knuckles and his gloves are on. He carries a pig of iron from Taerom's stack to the tailboard against his chest. He doesn't throw it up, he lays it on the bed, then goes back for the next.

The old one stands by the near wheel with a torn-out page flat against a board in one hand. His head is down. His lips move as each piece goes on.

The breeze off the forge shifts, and Copper's nose gets the men under the hot iron and horse. There's sweat, and wool that's been sweated in for days. Under that, faint and sharp, is grease with something bitter worked into it, a salve smell. And under the salve is something Copper doesn't have a picture for, only a twitch of dislike: old, healed-over burning, like hair singed a long time ago.

Then the young one lays a pig on the bed. James sees it from too far off to make out a slag ridge. The old one's lips stop.

He reads his page again. He looks at the bed, then at the stack in the yard. Taerom's plough-wright bar lies under its canvas by the lean-to, set apart from the rest. The old one looks at the canvas for a long moment. Then he turns his head to the smithy door. Taerom has come to stand in it with his arms folded and the forge-light behind him, and he says nothing at all.

The old man doesn't say anything either. He folds the page once along its old crease and puts it inside his coat. Then he lifts his head and looks along the street. He looks south first, down the Way towards the other forges. Then he looks north, up it, past the Red Bellows' window and the cat on its sill, towards the cooper's yard and the bend.

He isn't hurrying. He looks like a man who has found the count short and wants to know who's about before he decides what to do about it.

Copper looks back at him with mild interest and no fear at all. Behind the barrels and the sagging gable, James still can't be seen from the gate. Through the bond, faint but clear and very much beside the point, comes the cat's sense that the cloak coming down the street has sprats in it.

I stop where I am, short of the bend, and turn to the cooper's stacked barrels as if one of them might be the one I came for. I run a thumb along a hoop. A man comparing barrels.

Through the bond, gently: *Don't look at him. Look at the sprats.* Copper is good at that.

Then I round the bend at the same pace I've kept all morning, cross to the Red Bellows door without once turning my face toward the yard gate, and go in to my cup and my window. turns.reply:
James stops a few steps short of the bend and turns to the cooper's stack as if one of the barrels might be the one he came for. They're new oak, still pale, with the hoops driven tight. He runs his thumb along one hoop and feels the ridge where the iron was lapped and riveted.

Through the bond, gently: *Don't look at him. Look at the sprats.*

Copper doesn't need telling twice. The cat's gaze slides off the old man, unhurried, and comes to rest somewhere in the middle distance of the street, roughly where a cloak full of sprats ought to be. It's the blank, faraway look a cat gives a wall. Through it, at the edge of the cat's eyes, James can still see the yard gate.

The old one finishes looking north. He doesn't look back at the sill. He turns to the young one and says something short and low that doesn't carry across the street. The young one sets down the pig he has just picked up, wipes his gloves on his thighs and starts up the Way at a long, loose-jointed trot.

He's heading for the bend, straight towards James.

James keeps his thumb on the hoop. The boy comes round the cooper's gable at a jog with his eyes on the road ahead. Up close he's younger than he looked from the window, nineteen perhaps, with a sparse attempt at a beard and his shirt stuck dark to his back. As he passes he drags the back of one gloved hand across his forehead. The cuff of his sleeve slides back an inch.

Between the top of the glove and the edge of the sleeve there's a band of skin on the inside of his wrist, smooth and shiny and pinkish-white. It's old burn scar, long healed. James has seen plenty of burns, in camp kitchens and sacked villages and on the forearms of every smith in this town. Those were splashes and spatters with ragged edges. This one has a straight edge, cut as clean as a ruled line, and then the cuff falls back over it. The boy doesn't look at the man by the barrels. He trots on up the Way towards the temple square and is gone among the forges.

Back at the gate, through Copper's eyes, the old one has turned to his horses. He runs a gloved hand down the near horse's foreleg and lifts the hoof to look at it. That puts his head down.

James lets go of the hoop and rounds the bend at the same pace he has kept all morning.

The Red Bellows door is across the street and a little up from the yard gate. He walks to it in the open, through the cold mud, a man coming back to his cup, and he doesn't turn his face towards the dray once.

Copper is still watching the gate, and through him James sees what he won't turn his own head to see. The old one sets the hoof down. He doesn't straighten up all at once. He stays half bent with one hand on the horse's shoulder, and his eyes come up and follow James across the street, from the bend to the inn door. His expression doesn't change and he doesn't hurry, but he keeps looking the whole way. James feels it between his shoulder blades the way a cat feels a held breath.

The door of the Red Bellows closes behind him.

The common room is nearly empty now. James's cup is where he left it, cold, and the girl with flour on her arms has wiped the table round it. He sits at the window and takes the twist of sprats out of his cloak. The paper is greasy and the fish are still faintly warm. He unrolls it on the outer sill next to the cat.

Copper looks at the sprats, then at James, and then the bond fills with smoke and salt and a contentment so complete that it crowds out everything else. The cat eats them head first, one at a time, crunching.

Through the thick green glass, with his own eyes now, James can see the yard gate. The dray stands half loaded, with the young one's last pig lying on the ground by the tailboard where he put it down. The old one stands at the near horse's head and isn't loading. He has taken the folded page out of his coat again and holds it, unread, against his thigh. Taerom hasn't moved from his doorway. Neither of them has said a word since the boy ran off. They're waiting for somebody coming down from the temple square.

The girl with flour on her arms takes the cold cup without comment and comes back with a fresh one, steaming and sharp with clove. James puts a silver on the board and waves her off when she reaches into her apron for the change. She looks at the coin, then at him, and the coin goes into the apron pocket. She stays where she is, one hip against the next table.

She looks out through the green glass at the dray, and her mouth goes flat.

"Them? Never. Not a foot over the step." She wipes her hands down her forearms, which only moves the flour around. "First time they came, the young one stood out there and looked at our door like a dog looks at a butcher's. You could see him smelling it. The old one said something to him, one word, and he turned round and didn't look at it again." She shrugs. "I took a jug out after. Small beer, on the house, because it was hot and they'd been lifting. The old one shook his head without even looking at it. The horses got the trough. They didn't."

She picks up the empty plate from his breakfast.

"Three times now. Horses drink, men don't. My mam says that's chapel folk, some kind of fast." She plainly doesn't think much of her mam's idea. "Chapel folk say thank you." She goes off to the kitchen with the plate.

James settles his shoulder against the window frame, with the cup up where it hides half his face.

Nothing moves on the Way for a while. A farrier's boy goes past with a bundle of nail rod on his shoulder. The cooper comes out and rolls a barrel along his stack, and goes back in. On the sill Copper has finished the sprats and is washing his face slowly, one side and then the other, with his eyes half shut. Through the bond comes salt and warmth and nothing else.

Then the young one comes round the cooper's gable. He isn't trotting now. He walks a pace behind and to one side of a man in a dove-grey coat, the way a servant walks.

Master Aule picks his way down the street around the worst of the mud, the way the fish-woman said. He carries the little ledger shut in one hand. He doesn't look at the Red Bellows or the cat on its sill. He doesn't look at anything except the ground in front of his boots, until he reaches the yard gate.

The old one has straightened up from the horse. He steps in close as Aule arrives and says something short and low, close to his shoulder. Aule listens with his head tilted and his eyes on the open ledger. He nods once and doesn't look up.

Then he crosses to the lean-to, lifts one corner of the canvas with two fingers and looks at the bar stacked under it. He lets the canvas fall and turns to the smithy door.

Whatever he says doesn't carry across the street. Taerom's answer does.

"That's the plough-wright's. It's spoken for. It's not for sale." The smith hasn't unfolded his arms. "Weigh what's on your bed and count me the difference, or take your gold and go. I told you that's how it stands."

Aule says something else, just as quiet. Taerom shakes his head once.

Aule goes to the anvil. He doesn't argue. He opens the ledger flat on the anvil's horn, writes a line in it, and then picks coins off the pile one at a time and drops them into his purse. James counts eight from the window, perhaps nine, and he can't be sure of the last one. Aule shuts the ledger, tucks it into his coat and says one word to the old one over his shoulder. Then he walks back up the Way the way he came. He steps around the same puddles, and he still doesn't look at the Red Bellows.

The young one picks the pig up off the ground where he left it, holds it against his chest and lays it on the bed. Then he goes back for the next. The old one has the torn page out again, flat against its board. His lips are moving.

Taerom stands in his doorway until Aule has gone round the cooper's gable. Then he walks to the anvil and sweeps what's left of the gold into his apron with the side of his hand, all at once, the way you'd clear slag off a bench. He goes back inside without looking at the dray.

The stack in the yard is going down. From the size of what's left, there's perhaps half an hour of lifting before the bed is full and the pair are put to the road west.
