The young one carries pig after pig across the yard and lays each one on the bed. The old one keeps his page flat on the board and moves his lips over every piece. The cup cools slowly in James's hands. Across the street Taerom's hammer starts again. It's steady work, the sound of a man who has decided not to watch.

The stack under the canvas is gone a little before the fourth hour after noon. The young one lays the last pig on the bed, presses both gloved palms on it for a moment as if he were settling it, and climbs up onto the box. The old one reads his page through one last time, folds it on its crease and puts it inside his coat. He doesn't go into the smithy to say anything. He climbs up, takes the reins and clicks his tongue once, and the dark pair leans into the collars.

The dray doesn't go back south through town. It pulls out of the yard gate with a heavy grinding of loaded wheels, swings north up the Way for forty feet or so, and turns left at the corner past the Red Bellows. That corner is where the grey ruts give way to red. The turn brings it right under the window.

The young one is looking at the inn door again, the way the serving girl described it, until the dray carries him past it. The old one isn't looking at the door. As the box comes level with the window he turns his head, without hurry, and looks through the open shutter. He looks past the cat on the sill at the man behind the cup. It's a long, level look with nothing in it, the look of a man checking a face against one he already has. Then he faces the road again. The heavy shoes ring on the last of the cobbles and then go dull in the clay. The rumble goes off west between the hedges for a long while, getting smaller, until the street is only hammers and a dog barking somewhere behind the cooper's.

James finishes the cup.

*Stay. Watch the yard.* He gives Copper the lean-to, Hild's cart and the sleeping mule, then a stranger stopping at the gate or the inn door with questions. Last he gives the cat himself the way the cat knows him: the old cloak, the smell of the rod's polish, and his own walk as it looks from a sill. *Anyone who asks after this.*

Copper's ears turn back once to show he heard. Then the cat settles lower on the sill with his paws tucked under him, the shape a cat takes when it means to stay a long time.

---

The walk up the Way is the same one he made at noon. It's quieter now that the iron has gone. Past the cooper's bend the bond thins and goes still. Then the street opens out into the temple square, and the Song of the Morning rises over it.

The sun has moved round behind the temple and the gilded sunburst over the doors is in shadow. The doors stand open. Inside it's cooler than the street and smells of beeswax and lamp oil, and faintly of something green and bitter from deeper in the building. The windows high in the east wall are rose and amber glass. At this hour they let in very little light, and the nave lies in a soft dusk. An old woman kneels near the front. Halfway down the left wall a door stands open on a whitewashed room with cots in it.

The offering bowl stands just inside the doors on a stone pillar. It's beaten copper, worn smooth at the lip. A priest in a faded rose-coloured robe is sweeping wax drippings off the flags near it. He's a man of sixty or so, bald, with a fringe of white hair and a healer's forearms bare to the elbow, stained yellow-green at the fingertips. He looks up at the step behind him and watches the gold piece go into the bowl. It rings once against the copper.

He leans the broom against the pillar.

"That's generous for a man who hasn't asked for anything yet." His voice is low, pitched for a temple, but there's no reproach in it. "Brother Haskel. I keep the infirmary. What is it you need?"

He hears James out without interrupting. At the gloves his eyebrows go up a little. At the water he frowns. At the mine his face goes still for a moment, the way Hild's jaw stopped that morning, and then it moves on.

"Men who won't drink." He rubs his stained thumb across his fingertips. "That's no rite of ours. The Morninglord's people break their fast at dawn, and they don't refuse a cup from anyone who offers one. I don't know of any house that forbids water, not on this coast. A man refuses a cup when he's been told not to take one, or when he's afraid of what he'd owe for it. Either way somebody put that into him."

He turns his head towards the open door of the infirmary.

"Gloves in forge heat is a different matter. In this town, when a man keeps his hands covered at a forge, he's either hiding a burn or hiding a mark. Smiths aren't ashamed of burns." He pauses. "I make a salve in there for old burn scars, the kind that pull tight and crack in the cold. It's wormwood and tallow with a little pine tar. Bitter stuff. You can smell it from here, I expect. Most of the town buys a pot a winter, if that." He looks back at James. "Four days ago a woman bought eight. She paid in gold and didn't haggle. She was tall, with her hair cut short as a boy's. Somebody had broken her nose for her once, straight across. I asked her who it was for, because eight pots is a ward's worth. She said it was for a camp. Then she took them and went."

He lets that sit for a breath.

"The mine." He takes his time over it. "That's older than me. It's older than my teacher, too. A long time ago there was a trading concern out of the Gate that worked mines in the Cloakwood. The men in them weren't hired, they were taken. Some were bought, some came off the roads, some came out of debtors' cells. The mine was flooded in the end, and the concern broke, and the ones who could walk came out of the wood. A good many of them came here, because this was the nearest door with a priest behind it." He nods down the nave. "One of them left that."

Beside the infirmary door, in a shallow niche in the stone, an iron shackle hangs from a peg. It's a single cuff with a broken length of chain, black and plain. There's no dust on it. There's no rust either, not on the cuff, not on the chain, not in the deep stamped mark on the outer face of the iron. The mark is a circle with a single straight bar cut through it, like a coin someone tried to halve.

"Nobody oils it," Brother Haskel says. "Nobody's oiled it in all the years I've been here, and it hangs a few feet from a room full of wet poultices. The man who left it never said what the mark was. The book says he wouldn't say."

He picks up the broom again and doesn't start sweeping.

"The infirmary book for that year is in the undercroft, if the mice have left it. It lists who came in and what was wrong with them. It'll take me the rest of the light to find it." He looks at James for a long moment. "Do you want me to look?"

"Candles, then." He leans the broom back against the pillar. "Before the doors shut. That's the second hour after dark. I'll have it by then or I'll tell you the mice won."

James walks down the nave. The old woman near the front doesn't look round. His boots make no sound on the flags, and the green, bitter smell from the infirmary gets stronger as he goes.

The shackle hangs at about chest height. It's one cuff, hinged, as wide as three fingers, with the pin hole worn oval from use. Four links of chain hang from it. The last one is broken, not cut. It's been pulled open and twisted, so somebody, at some point, wrenched on it until the iron gave. The stamp sits on the outer face where a guard would see it: a ring, and through the ring one straight bar, struck deep and clean, the edges as sharp as the day the die came down. He studies it the way he studied Taerom's hammer and cloud that morning. Then he lets the other sense reach out, the one the goddess left in him, and feels for the cold spot in the room.

There's something there. He can feel it, the way you feel someone standing behind a door. But it gives him nothing. When he leans on it there's no shape to it, no school, no warmth or chill he could put a name to, and he can't tell whether it lives in the iron, in the stamp or in the broken link. It stays shut. Whatever was put into this cuff was put in by someone who knew more than he does, and it has kept to itself for a long time.

Behind him the broom has stopped. Brother Haskel has come halfway down the nave and stands a few steps off with his arms folded under his robe. He doesn't come closer to the niche than that.

"Burns," he says. "But not the way you mean." He takes his time over it. "I've only my teacher's telling, not the book. He was a boy when the man came in. He said it was the hands. Both palms, burned smooth, old burns, the kind you get from holding something hot for too long, not from splashes. And the mark on the wrist, there." He nods at the stamp without looking at it. "The same mark, burned in."

He rubs his stained thumb slowly across his fingertips.

"And he wouldn't take a cup. That's the other thing my teacher remembered. For the first tenday he wouldn't drink from anything he was handed. He went to the trough in the yard at night with his hands, like a horse." He looks at James then. "I'd forgotten that until you asked about the wagon men. I'd rather not have remembered it."

He looks at the shackle a moment longer, as if it might add something. It doesn't.

"The book will say more, or it won't. My teacher was a boy." He turns towards a low door in the right-hand wall, where narrow stone steps go down into the dark, and takes a lamp off its hook. "Second hour after dark. Come to the side door if the front's barred. Knock twice."

The light through the rose and amber glass has gone thin and low. Somewhere outside a cart goes past in the square. The shackle hangs in its niche, with no dust and no rust on it.

James nods to the priest and leaves the shackle hanging in its niche. Brother Haskel has already gone down the narrow stair with the lamp. The light goes down the steps ahead of him, and then the low doorway is dark.

Outside, the sunburst over the doors is still in shadow, and the square has started to empty for the evening. Two of the four horses have gone from the rail. The fish-woman is tying a cloth over her crock. Across the mud, Feldepost's glazed windows hold the sky, which is already turning a paler late-afternoon blue. Nothing behind them moves that he can see. He stands on the step long enough for the bitter green smell to leave his nose, then goes down into the square.

The walk down the Way is the same one again, but the shadows have changed sides. The forges on the left are in shade now. The Silver Tongs is still cold. The Holloways' boy has given up on his cradle and gone somewhere. James rounds the cooper's bend, and a few steps on the bond fills in.

Copper is on the sill where he was left, still a loaf, paws tucked. He's pleased with himself in the quiet way of a cat that has stayed exactly where it was told to and wants that noticed.

The report doesn't come in order. A cat doesn't keep time. It comes the way a cat remembers things, by what mattered.

Hild comes first, because she was the biggest thing in the yard. She finished unloading, sack after sack onto the stack under the lean-to. Then she backed the empty cart in beside it, took the mule out of the traces and gave it the trough and a nosebag. Copper didn't think much of the nosebag: oats, nothing interesting. After that she went off down the Way south with a bundle under her arm, and she hasn't come back. The cart is still under the lean-to and the mule is dozing next to it.

Taerom came out once. He stood in the empty yard where the stack had been, looked at the bare ground for a while and went back in. His hammer has been going ever since.

Then the cat's attention sharpens, and James feels it like a held breath.

Someone came to the Bellows door. It wasn't the old one or Aule. It was a boy, younger than the wagon boy, in a clean apron. He came down the Way from the north, walking quickly like someone sent on an errand who wants to get it over with. Copper doesn't care about the boy's face. He cares about the boy's smell, and he puts it in front of James whole: kitchen grease, boot-black, and under them, faint, the thing Copper lost in the temple square that morning. Good wool, ink and that clean, bitter rich man's soap. The boy hadn't touched the grey-coat, but he'd been in a room where the grey-coat had been. He was carrying it in his clothes.

He didn't go in. He stood on the step and called, and the girl with flour on her arms came out, wiping her hands. They talked. Copper didn't follow the words and didn't try. What he kept is what she did with her hands. She looked at the window seat, which was empty, with a cold cup on the table and a cat outside it. She shrugged. Then she said something short, tipped her chin up once towards the upper floor, and shook her head. The boy nodded, said one more thing, and went back up the Way the way he'd come. That was a while before the bond came back. Somewhere in the hour James was inside the temple, the boy went up the Way and James came down it, and they never passed.

The girl stood on the step a moment after he'd gone, looking at the window seat. Then she looked at the cat. Then she went back in.

Nothing else. Nobody with the old one's shoulders, nobody in dove-grey. A dog went by twice.

The last thing that comes over the bond is the sun gone off the sill, the stone going cool under his belly, and a clear, unembarrassed image of a sprat.

Through the green glass the common room is filling for supper. Carters are coming in out of the yard, and somebody is laughing at the hearth. The girl is moving between the tables with a tray. James's cold cup has been cleared away. Over the rooftops the sky has started to yellow. There's an hour and more of daylight left, then dusk, and two knocks at a side door after that.

turns.message:
I take the sprat under advisement and go in.

The common room's warm and loud now, which suits me. I find a place at the end of the board near the kitchen door rather than my window seat, and when the girl with flour on her arms comes past with her tray I catch her sleeve, lightly, and put a silver on the wood beside my hand where she can see it.

"The boy who came to the door this afternoon. Clean apron, from up the square." I keep my voice under the noise. "What did he ask, exactly — and what did you tell him?" A beat, not unkind. "I'm not angry. I'd just like to know how much of me he carried back up the hill."
turns.reply:
Copper watches him go in. Over the bond comes the sprat again, smaller this time, then a cat's flat patience. He doesn't move off the sill.

Inside, the Red Bellows has filled up for supper. Carters crowd the long boards, a smith's crew still in their aprons has the hearth, and someone has started an argument about a horse that nobody is going to win. The air is thick with mutton fat and wet wool. James takes the end of the board by the kitchen door, where the noise is loudest and nobody looks at the man sitting there.

The girl comes past with a tray of bowls on her shoulder. He touches her sleeve lightly and she stops. She sees the silver on the wood beside his hand before she looks at him. She sets the tray on the board's edge, puts one bowl in front of a carter who didn't order it and doesn't complain, and leans in so she doesn't have to shout.

"Didn't think you'd seen him." She glances at the window, where the cat's shape sits against the yellowing sky. "Ah. The cat, then. My mam would have something to say about that."

She takes the coin and it goes into her apron with the other.

"He asked was there a man stopping here, in an old green-grey cloak, that had sat at the window all morning. I said there was. He asked your name." She shrugs, the same shrug Copper saw from the sill. "I don't know it. Master Pell keeps the book, not me, and I told him so. Then he asked were you in. I said no, you'd gone up the Way after the wagon left and I hadn't seen you back." She tips her chin at the ceiling. "He asked was it a front room or a back one. I said back. I shouldn't have, I suppose. It didn't seem much."

Someone at the hearth bangs a cup for more. She ignores it.

"Then he asked how long you were stopping. I said I didn't know, that's the master's book again. And he said thank you, which is more than the wagon men ever did, and went." She frowns a little, thinking it over. "He didn't ask for Master Pell. I'd have thought he would, if it was your name he wanted. He just went straight back up the hill like he'd got what he came for."

She picks up her tray and steadies it on her shoulder, then doesn't go.

"He's Feldepost's boy. Tam. He runs their errands, he's harmless." A pause while she looks at James properly, the way she looked at the cat. "But whoever sent him isn't Feldepost's. They don't send down here asking after our lodgers." She shifts the tray. "If he comes back, do you want me to tell him different?"

I shake my head. "No. Don't lie for me. Tam's harmless, but whoever sent him isn't, and I'd rather they were short with you than I was the reason they weren't." I let go of her sleeve. "If he comes back, tell him the truth — you saw me come in, eat, and go up. And if he asks how long I'm stopping, say the same you said before: it's the master's book."

I glance up at the ceiling, at the back room with my pack and crossbow in it, then at the kitchen door behind her.

"Two things more, and then I'll let you feed them." I put another silver on the wood. "Is there a way out of this house that isn't the front door? A yard gate, the kitchen, anything that comes out somewhere other than the Way. And would Master Pell think it very strange if a lodger paid for a back room tonight and slept in a different one?"
turns.reply:
The girl hears him out with the tray steadied on her shoulder. When he says not to lie for him, she gives him a quick look, as if she'd been ready to argue and has decided not to. The third silver goes into her apron with the other two.

"In, ate, went up. Master's book." She nods once. "I can say that and it'll be true."

She jerks her chin at the kitchen door behind her. It's propped open on a wedge, and through it comes heat, the hiss of fat and a woman's voice telling somebody to mind the pot.

"Through the kitchen, then the scullery, and you're in the back yard. There's the well and the privy, and the stable where the carters put up. The yard gate goes onto the lane behind. Turn right and the lane comes out on the red track, past the corner, so you're west of the house and nobody on the Way sees you." She thinks about it. "Mind, Dobbin bars the gate at full dark and sleeps in the stable. He's the ostler's boy. Lift the bar and he'll wake, and he'll want to know who you are. He's no harm. He just likes to know."

Somebody at the hearth bangs a cup again. She still ignores it.

"Master Pell." Her mouth goes flat, the way it did over the wagon men, though this time it's nearer to fondness. "He'd think it strange. He'd still take your money." She looks over at the tap, where a heavyset man of fifty or so in a leather waistcoat is drawing ale with one hand and making a mark on a slate with the other. "The drover who had the front room over the street went south this morning, so it's empty. It costs more and it's noisier. Carts start under the window before the bell." She shrugs under the tray. "But you'll have to ask him. It's his book. I only carry the plates."

She lifts the tray an inch higher and finally goes. She puts a bowl down in front of the man who's been banging his cup, and he stops.

Through the window, against the yellowing sky, Copper hasn't moved off the sill. The bond brings the cooling stone and a patient sense that the sprat question is still on the table.

Over at the tap, Master Pell finishes his mark on the slate, wipes his hands on his waistcoat and looks round the room the way an innkeeper counts heads at supper.

note.text:
**Note from James's player**

**What worked**

The town. That's the main thing. Hild, Taerom, the fish-woman, the serving girl — every one of them answered from where they actually stood, not from where my question wanted them to stand. Hild made me say what the wood was to me before she'd give me a seat, and then made me promise to give way beside her mule. Taerom didn't take the gold, then did take most of it, because he has nails owed. That's a world that runs on its own, which is what the brief promised.

Copper. The eel, the "from me, not fed" distinction, the failed trail at the temple square played as a cat who doesn't think it's his fault — all of it was right. The hundred-foot limit on the bond was honoured and actually mattered to how I moved around town. Good.

The clue drip. Gloves in a forge, shoes with long calkins, a satchel heavy in and light out, eight pots of burn salve, a shackle that doesn't rust. Each conversation gave me one concrete thing I could carry in my head. I never felt fed, and I never felt starved. The old driver's level look through the window did more than a fight would have.

No wasted rolls. One die in the whole session, where it belonged. The GM telling me "nothing was uncertain" was the right call every time.

**What broke**

The clock. The tracker read "midday" through the entire morning and the GM apologised for it three times. Then it read "afternoon" while the noon bell was ringing. Small, but it's noise on every turn.

My second message mixed a "?" note with an action, and the GM refused the whole thing — nothing moved, I had to resend. Either the app should accept mixed messages or the GM could answer the question and play the action in one go. It cost a turn for nothing.

The Arcana card applied +2 when my sheet says +3. The GM caught it, and it wouldn't have changed the result, but the card should read the sheet.

The out-of-game recaps ("none of the four needed a roll, here's how each came out") restate the narration I just read, at length, every turn. One line would do. They made each reply a third longer than it needed to be.

**What was missing**

Tymora. She's my patron and the reason I'm in Beregost at all. The coin on my chest is warm; nobody said so once. I spent a whole day in and out of a tavern and never saw a hand of cards being dealt. That's the obvious tug, and it's on my sheet as something the GM may use. Not every session, but a session with this much sitting at tables was the place for it.

A cost. Everything I bought was bought with silver and copper. The look through the window and Tam asking after my room are the first hints of a price, and they came in the last ten minutes. Fine for a first session — I'd rather it build — but the next one should collect.

A clean stopping point. I'm standing between Master Pell's book and two knocks on a side door after dark, with first light and Hild's cart behind that. Whoever picks this up needs: the front room question unasked, Haskel's book unread, the sprat still owed.

I'd sit at this table again.

after.text:
Yes. Two.

The first was at the window, when the dray turned under it and the old one looked at me. I wanted to look back. Taerom had told me not to, and I'd said I wouldn't, so I kept the cup up and let the cat do the looking — but there was a half-second where James the soldier wanted to meet that stare and let the man know he'd been seen seeing. I think it was right not to. I'm not sure. A man who checks your face against one he already has might respect being checked back, or might decide the question's answered. I chose not to find out, and I still don't know what it would have cost either way.

The second was smaller and I'm less proud of it. In the common room at supper, when the girl said Tam had asked which room I was in and whether I was stopping long — I wanted to go up to Feldepost's then and there. Walk in, ask for Master Aule by name, sit down across from him and see what a man who weighs iron does when the thing he's been weighing walks in and introduces itself. I had the face for it; I could have worn a different one if I'd wanted. I didn't go because I'd given Haskel two gold and a promise, and because Hild's cart is at first light and I'd rather be on it than explaining myself to the Fist. But that was the move the character wanted, and I talked him out of it with the calendar.

If there's a third, it's the cards. Not that I wanted to play — but every time the GM put me at a board with a silver on the wood, there was a beat where I noticed no one had offered a hand, and I was glad. That gladness is the character's weakness showing, and I didn't say so out loud. Should have.

opening.text:
Light slips through the gaps in the shutter and lies in thin gold bars across the blanket. Somewhere down the street a hammer strikes iron, then another, then a dozen. Beregost is a town of smiths, and it wakes loudly. A temple bell rolls over the rooftops. Downstairs a door bangs, a pan hisses, and someone laughs too early in the day.

The room is as you left it. The studded leather hangs over the chair, and the crossbow leans against the chest. The purse at the bedside is heavy with about three hundred and fifty gold, the last of that winning hand. Your pack lies beside it, and somewhere inside is a deck of cards you have not touched since.

The cat is not asleep. It sits on the windowsill with its nose to the gap in the shutter, ears forward, tail twitching slowly. Something in the street has caught its interest. Through the bond you feel its attention, sharp and unhurried, and no worry in it.

No one is waiting for you. No contract, no march, no debt due by noon, only the smell of breakfast, the noise of a working town and a whole day with nothing written on it. The cat turns its head and looks at you, as if asking what comes first.
